blocks.text: 1. Incremental Ingestion

blocks.alt: A source change goes through incremental ingestion to produce an updated index

blocks.text: Incremental Ingestion covers how a pipeline keeps its collection current over time, closing out the Document Ingestion module by tying every earlier topic together.
It updates an existing collection instead of rebuilding it from scratch every time.
2. Full Rebuilds Versus Incremental Updates

blocks.alt: A full rebuild is compared against an incremental update

blocks.text: A full rebuild reprocesses every document; an incremental update touches only what changed.
As a collection grows, full rebuilds become too slow and too expensive to repeat often.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Cost as the collection grows"],"rows":[["Full rebuild","Reprocesses every document, growing slower over time"],["Incremental update","Touches only new, changed, or removed documents"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Detecting What Changed

blocks.alt: A previous snapshot is diffed against the current state

blocks.text: Comparing a source's current state against the last ingested state reveals what is new, changed, or removed.
Database Ingestion covers keeping ingested data synchronized, and the same detection challenge applies broadly here too.
4. Handling New Documents

blocks.alt: A new document gets added to the index

blocks.text: A new document simply gets ingested and added to the collection.
This is the simplest of the three cases an incremental pipeline has to handle.
5. Handling Updated Documents
An updated document needs its old chunks removed before the new version is ingested.
Leaving stale chunks behind lets outdated information keep surfacing in retrieval.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Ingesting an updated document without removing its old chunks leaves both the outdated and the current version retrievable at once, letting a retrieval system surface stale, contradictory information.

blocks.text: 6. Handling Deleted Documents

blocks.alt: A deleted document gets removed from the index

blocks.text: A deleted source document needs its chunks removed from the collection too.
Forgetting deletions leaves retrievable content for material that no longer exists.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Change type","Required action"],"rows":[["New document","Ingest and add to the collection"],["Updated document","Remove old chunks, then ingest the new version"],["Deleted document","Remove its chunks from the collection entirely"]]}

blocks.text: 7. Scheduling Ingestion Runs
Running incremental ingestion on a regular schedule keeps the collection reliably current.
API Ingestion covers polling versus webhooks, and the same two scheduling options apply here too.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A well scheduled incremental ingestion run balances freshness against cost: running too rarely lets the collection go stale, while running too often wastes resources reprocessing sources that have not actually changed.

blocks.text: 8. Incremental Ingestion As The Final Step
Every technique covered across this module feeds into keeping the collection both complete and current.
This closes out the Document Ingestion module before Chunking, covered next.
9. Recognizing When Incremental Ingestion Matters Most

blocks.alt: A source changing frequently points toward incremental ingestion

blocks.text: Large, frequently changing collections need incremental ingestion.
A small, static, rarely changing source, by contrast, can rely on occasional full rebuilds.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates detecting new, updated, and deleted documents between two ingestion runs.

code.content:
previous_state = {
    "doc1": {"hash": "abc123", "chunks": ["doc1_chunk1", "doc1_chunk2"]},
    "doc2": {"hash": "def456", "chunks": ["doc2_chunk1"]},
}

current_source = {
    "doc1": "abc123",  # unchanged
    "doc2": "xyz999",  # updated, hash changed
    "doc3": "ghi789",  # new document
}

def incremental_sync(previous_state, current_source):
    # compare current source state against the previous ingestion
    new_docs = [doc_id for doc_id in current_source if doc_id not in previous_state]
    updated_docs = [
        doc_id for doc_id in current_source
        if doc_id in previous_state and previous_state[doc_id]["hash"] != current_source[doc_id]
    ]
    deleted_docs = [doc_id for doc_id in previous_state if doc_id not in current_source]
    return new_docs, updated_docs, deleted_docs

new_docs, updated_docs, deleted_docs = incremental_sync(previous_state, current_source)

print("New documents:", new_docs)
print("Updated documents:", updated_docs)
print("Deleted documents:", deleted_docs)

for doc_id in updated_docs + deleted_docs:
    print(f"Removing stale chunks for {doc_id}: {previous_state[doc_id]['chunks']}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows one unchanged document skipped, one updated document flagged for its stale chunks to be removed, and one new document queued for ingestion.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Running a full rebuild on every ingestion cycle even as the collection grows large.
Ingesting an updated document without removing its old, now stale chunks first.
Forgetting to remove chunks for documents that have been deleted at the source.
Scheduling ingestion runs either far too rarely or far too frequently for the source's actual rate of change.
